question: A 36-year-old primigravid woman comes to the physician for a prenatal visit at 14 weeks' gestation. She has had episodic headaches over the past month. At home, blood pressure measurements have ranged from 134/82 mm Hg to 148/94 mm Hg. Today, her blood pressure is 146/91 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 13-week gestation. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, serum ALT is 17 U/L, and platelet count is 320,000/mm3. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Elevated blood pressure readings" -> "Consistent with hypertension" -> "Consider hypertensive disorders of pregnancy" -> 80% CHAIN: "Elevated blood pressure readings" -> "No proteinuria on urinalysis" -> "Excludes preeclampsia" -> 70% CHAIN: "Elevated blood pressure readings" -> "Normal serum creatinine, ALT, and platelet count" -> "Less likely to be chronic hypertension" -> 75% CHAIN: "Elevated blood pressure readings" -> "Uterus size consistent with gestational age" -> "Supports gestational hypertension" -> 85% CHAIN: "Elevated blood pressure readings" -> "No proteinuria on urinalysis" -> "Excludes eclampsia" -> 70% CHAIN: "Elevated blood pressure readings" -> "Systolic blood pressure consistently elevated" -> "Consider isolated systolic hypertension" -> 80%
analysis: The patient's presentation with elevated blood pressure after 20 weeks of gestation, along with episodic headaches and no significant proteinuria, is most consistent with a diagnosis of gestational hypertension. This condition typically resolves postpartum without progressing to preeclampsia.
